# Summary {#part-adaptation-summary .unnumbered}

Post-training starts from a base model that has broad capability but lacks the behavior a product needs. Demonstrations, adapters, behavior specifications, preference comparisons, reward models, direct preference objectives, verifiable rewards, safety policies, and synthetic data loops all try to specify which behavior the model should keep. They differ in optimizer and pipeline, but all of them depend on a signal that tells the model what better means.

That signal can fail in three ways. When it is underspecified, the model learns the surface style of preferred answers and misses the substantive requirement. When it is exploitable, the model learns to game the reward. When the judge that scores outputs is weak, the loop can overfit to it, so its own metrics can look improved while actual behavior has not improved. The part therefore treats alignment as the governance of signals, reviewers, filters, verifiers, and policy text.

The rest of the book asks the same four questions of every signal: who wrote it, how it is checked, where it fails, and when the system is allowed to trust its own output. The open question is how far synthetic data, AI feedback, and verifiers can push improvement before the judge, filter, or policy becomes the new ceiling. Part IV asks what can be left to inference time instead of being frozen into weights: search, verification, tool calls, traces, and extra computation spent only when a request seems to need it.
